keyVerseText: And there was a great famine in Samaria: and, behold, they besieged it, until an ass's head was sold for fourscore pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung for five pieces of silver.
rootMeaning: The root of קַב (qab) is connected to the verb קָבַב (qâbab), which carries the idea of scooping out or cursing. This etymology suggests a notion of measurement or separation by hollowing or scooping, which is fitting for a noun that denotes a hollow vessel used for measuring dry goods. The literal sense of a scooped-out container enriches the English gloss of 'cab' by emphasizing its physical form and function as a measured capacity rather than just an abstract unit.
usageInScripture: The word קַב appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, specifically in 2 Kings 6:25, where it is translated as a dry measure of capacity. The limited occurrence and consistent translation as a unit of measure highlight its precise technical use in describing quantities of dry substances. This singular usage underscores the term's specificity and importance for understanding ancient measures related to daily life and economic conditions.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding קַב as a measure of capacity rooted in the concept of scooping out provides insight into the tangible realities behind biblical narratives, especially those involving provision and scarcity. The measure reflects God's concern for the daily needs of His people and the tangible aspects of sustenance. In the Christian faith, this reminds believers that God's provision is both practical and measured, sustaining His people even in times of famine or trial. It also invites reflection on the sufficiency of God's provision, whether abundant or limited, as He governs all circumstances.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Kings 6:25, the word קַב is used to describe a quarter part of a cab of dove's dung being sold for five pieces of silver during a severe famine in Samaria. This measure highlights the extreme scarcity and desperation of the time, as even such an unlikely commodity was traded at high cost. The use of קַב here quantifies the severity of the famine, showing how every small portion was precious, and thus deepening the reader's understanding of the dire conditions faced by the people.
